extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; legislators and constitutional thinkers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical guidance for assessing and designing constitutions, distribution of public offices, and the role of laws versus rulers, drawn from classical political theory. Focuses on who should hold which powers, how laws relate to constitutions, and remedies for excessive pre-eminence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited popular power with safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: The freemen who compose the bulk of the people should have absolute power in some things, but it is not safe to trust them with the first offices in the state on account of their iniquity and their ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit the many to vote in public assemblies and to determine causes, and give them the power of electing officers and inquiring into their conduct when out of office, but prevent them from themselves being the chief magistrates. Example rationale: the multitude when collected have sufficient understanding for these purposes and are useful when mixing among higher ranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve highest offices for those fit by property/virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unsafe to entrust the first offices in the state to the many because they are neither men of property nor uniformly virtuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great officers, treasurers, generals, etc., should be taken from men of great fortune and worth; property, family, and proven fidelity often justify claims to higher office where those qualities are relevant to the office's duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialist selection by practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: To elect a proper person in any science is the business of those who are skilful therein; as in geometry, of geometricians; in steering, of steersmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an office requires technical knowledge or skill, selection and judgment should rest with those knowledgeable in that art (physicians judge physicians, architect judges mason). Anti-pattern: allowing non-experts to choose technical officers leads to poor appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective judgement can outperform individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Although each individual may know less than specialists, when they come together they will know things better, or at least not worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use assemblies and collective deliberation for matters where aggregated judgement is advantageous; analogy: a public entertainment is better than one man's portion. Caveat: collectives are still fallible and can be misled by passions, but are less easily corrupted by bribery than single individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign offices by relevant merit (fitness for office)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employments of the state ought to be given according to those qualifications which are useful to the business in hand, not according to unrelated excellences like complexion, height, family, or beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the best flute must be given to the best flautist, not the man of best family; superiority in unrelated qualities should not confer claim to office. Avoid comparing incommensurable excellences (bodily strength vs virtue) to justify office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue and education as necessary bases for civic office
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue and education most justly claim the right of being considered as the necessary means of making the citizens happy; justice (a virtue) should have precedence in public honors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and offices should favour those whose virtue and education contribute to the common good; justice is necessary for a state's existence and valour for its happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should be calculated for citizens equal in nature and power
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of laws must be calculated for those who are equal to each other in nature and power; such eminent individuals are not the object of ordinary law because 'they are themselves a law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design laws aimed at the ordinary body of citizens; exceptional persons (those vastly superior in virtue or political ability) may require special treatment, since applying ordinary penalties to them would be unjust or absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ostracism to check pre-eminence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is any acknowledged difference in the power of citizens, it may be politically just to employ ostracism—banishing or restraining those who are too great—to preserve equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ostracism may be a remedy when certain individuals gain excessive weight in government (power, fortune, friendships). Historical examples: Periander's leveling of ears of corn; Athenians' treatment of subject states. Warning: in corrupt states ostracism can be weaponized by sedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional virtue may justify perpetual rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If pre-eminence is due to virtue rather than power or fortune, it may be natural and proper for such persons quietly to govern perpetually as kings in separate states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pre-eminence stems from outstanding virtue, neither banishment nor normal governance may be appropriate; exceptional rulers may stand above ordinary laws on account of their superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate forms of monarchy by distribution and limits of royal power
rubrics_metrics.description: Different species of monarchy (hereditary generalship, barbarian despotic monarchy under law, elective tyranny/aesymnetes, absolute monarch) should be distinguished and evaluated according to how much power the king holds and whether it is legally constrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the king governs by law, whether his guards are citizens or foreigners, whether his power is lifetime or temporary, and whether the kingship arose by benefit to the people (heroic origins) or by force. These distinctions affect legitimacy and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question permanence of high command (general for life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether it is advantageous for the office of general to continue in one person for life and whether it should be confined to particular families or be generally eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh stability and expertise of lifelong generals against risks of concentration of military command; consider eligibility rules (hereditary vs elective) and relation to the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer government by good laws over rule by single will
rubrics_metrics.description: It is preferable that law (reason without desire) govern rather than the will of an individual, because laws are less subject to passions and partiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws lay down general rules and provide stability; where laws cannot speak to particulars, magistrates decide; but the general principle is that law is superior to arbitrary will. Example: a written law gives the mean and protects against rulers' passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow magistrates discretion where written law is silent
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates or authorised persons should be empowered to determine cases which the laws cannot particularly speak to, because written laws cannot foresee every particular circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame laws to cover general cases, but authorise magistrates to adapt in particulars; ensure magistrates act as servants/guardians of the law, and that their discretion is limited by law's principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer many good rulers to one good ruler when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If many persons equal in virtue exist, an aristocracy of good men is preferable to rule by a single good man, though unity may be necessary when such a number cannot be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many virtuous rulers provide diversity of counsel and are less likely to be corrupted by passion than one; historical note: early governments were monarchies because virtuous few were rare; when many virtuous equals appear they tend to prefer equality and free government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance the king's coercive power so he is superior to individuals but inferior to the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: A king ought to have proper power—sufficient to make him superior to any one person or even a large part of the community, but inferior to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the monarch has enough force to enforce law and maintain order (e.g., guards for protection), without becoming absolutely sovereign over the entire state; this balance protects against both anarchy and despotism.
